title: “Does trend following work?”
snippet:
“Does trend following work?”

A better quant question is:

“What kind of payoff structure does trend following create, and when does it fail?”

In this article, I tested a simple moving average crossover strategy on USDJPY.

The result was mixed:

60-min signals had no clear edge
240-min signals looked better
but the 2025 out-of-sample result failed
the strategy depended heavily on a few large winners
the long-side profit was hard to distinguish from simple Buy & Hold exposure

This is exactly why quant traders do not trust a backtest just because the equity curve looks good.

You need to test the structure behind the profit.

💙 This post is a very well-structured piece of practical quant content.

It accurately highlights some of the most common mistakes in crypto trading—overtrading, overfitting, and relying on a single coin—while emphasizing the importance of risk management and diversification.

What I particularly liked

• Basket Approach
Although AVAX delivered the best performance, the strategy wisely acknowledges the reality that no one knows which asset will outperform in the future. Diversifying through a basket approach is a smart way to manage risk, especially in crypto markets where trends can shift rapidly.

• Realistic View on Fees
It does an excellent job of showing how trading fees can become a significant cost when using leverage on perpetual DEXs such as Hyperliquid. The insight that "trading more is not an opportunity, but a cost" is particularly valuable.

• Out-of-Sample Validation
The clear separation between the optimization period and the testing period demonstrates a genuine effort to minimize overfitting, which adds credibility to the strategy.

A few points of caution

• Crypto markets experience extreme regime shifts between bull, bear, and sideways conditions. As a result, a dataset consisting of only six months of training data and 2.5 months of testing data may not be sufficient to prove long-term robustness. This is especially true if the 2025–2026 period was unusually volatile.

title: Staying on the Horse
snippet:
Staying on the Horse

I'll try and share a potentially useful lesson about trading. There's an idea, I call "Sound Smart Capital". It sounds smart to have 50 factors in one strategy. It sounds smart to have 30 reasons why you think a stock will go up.

In reality - this is not the case.

It's important to understand why this is true. When you have an edge - a lot of the time, it takes a while to even *know* you have an edge. Anyone can run a backtest but it takes a bit to figure out if you're making dough.

The more factors you add to a strategy - whether qualitative or quantitative, the longer it takes for you to figure out if you've got something viable. And the longer it takes to figure that out, the more likely you are to fully fail (have to get a job, get kicked out of fund etc)

"I can just isolate my factors". In practice this isn't really true. Because we move the markets when we trade. So if you're paper trading a factor you really have no idea if it works or not. And if you've got 5 factors in a quant trading strategy, in all likelihood they're cancelling each other out and preventing you from actually trading

Similarly with a qualitative trading strategy if you have a 15 pronged bull case for a stock and 10 of them play out and 5 of them don't, then the stock drops a lot - what have you learned? title: WEEKEND R&D:
snippet:
WEEKEND R&D:
"stop asking if an alpha passes a test... start asking how much it shrinks" was my starting point.. then I started thinking about Quant v Retail...

TLDR: Whether you are using someone else's "system" from a paid substack or your own... you should at least attempt to validate them/it...

Quant models or retail TA have the same issue...the backtest is overfit (like what LLMs are doing to benchmarks now lol)

Most Quants stop at pass/fail CV...
*me...I WANT A SHRINKAGE FUNCTION*

Pass fail is a category error

Pass fail CV asks:
"Is this alpha acceptable"
*But markets are continuous
overfitting is continuous
decay is continuous

Alphas do not flip from real to fake ....they shrink... 

A shrinkage function answers:
GIVEN WHAT I SAW IN SAMPLE...WHAT SHOULD I EXPECT OUT OF SAMPLE?
*oh your 21D MA crossover strategy you want to charge me $50/month for works from 2020-2025... ok lets test it...

The 2014 CSCV PBO paper is framed as strategy selection..
"pick best of N and ask if selection is overfit"

my project uses it differently...
ALPHA VALIDATION... NOT PORTFOLIO CONSTRUCTION

What you could do:
-Run CSCV per alpha across time blocks
-for each symmetric split you compute IS metric and OOS metric
-you return empirical samples of the conditional distribution

Now quantify the mapping:
*OOS = a + b·IS
-b is the expected haircut
-R² is stability

Add curvature:
*OOS = a + b1·IS + b2·IS²
-b2 negative means the prettier -the backtest the faster it decays

RETAIL USE: yo
